title: Fitting a decorative wood panel below a dado rail
subtitle: Fix an MDF or tongue-and-groove wood panel to the lower wall section below a dado rail for a period or contemporary panelled look
excerpt: How to fit a decorative panel to the lower wall section between a dado rail and the skirting. Covers marking the panel positions, fixing battens, fitting the panel sections, and painting.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for interior joinery finishes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A decorative panel fitted to the lower section of an interior wall, between the dado rail and the skirting board. Traditionally raised-and-fielded timber panels in period houses; modern versions use flat MDF with a chamfered or ovolo moulding as a frame. Also called wainscoting.
A thin strip of timber screwed to the wall face as a substrate for panels, plasterboard, or sheet goods. Provides a fixing point and a level plane where the wall surface is uneven.

content.text: covers the wall below the dado rail with a sheet of MDF or a series of tongue-and-groove boards, then frames the sections with a small moulding to give the appearance of raised panels. The job is mark, batten, cut, fix, fill, and paint. No complex joinery; the moulding does the detail work.

Sweep a cable-and-pipe detector across the lower wall section before fixing any battens. Cables and pipes run vertically and horizontally from sockets and switches. Mark any hits and plan batten positions to avoid them.

(25 x 50 mm planed timber) at the top and bottom of the panel zone, with one intermediate batten in the middle of the run if the panel height is more than 600 mm. Use the spirit level to keep each batten horizontal. Fix with 65 mm No. 8 screws into wall plugs in masonry, or directly into studs on a stud wall.
Cut and fix the panel sheet

Cut the MDF sheet to fit between the dado rail and the skirting, and between the corners or door openings. MDF cuts cleanly with a circular saw or jigsaw; keep the face side up and use a fine-tooth blade to reduce chipping. Fix to the battens with 40 mm No. 6 screws or 40 mm panel pins, countersinking the screw heads slightly below the surface. Fill the countersink holes and any edge gaps with a fine surface filler.

Mark out the panel rectangles on the MDF face. Cut the moulding (ovolo or chamfer-and-bead pattern, 18-25 mm face width) with 45-degree mitres at the corners using the mitre box. Fix the moulding strips with wood glue and 20 mm panel pins. Punch the pin heads slightly below the surface and fill. The moulding frame defines the panels and gives the look of raised-and-fielded work without the joinery.

Fill all pin holes, filler, and any gaps at the dado rail and skirting edges with a fine surface filler. Sand when dry with 120-grit, then 180-grit. Apply one coat of water-based wood primer, sand lightly when dry, then apply two coats of water-based eggshell or satin paint in the same colour as the skirting and dado rail. Apply decorator's caulk to any fine gap at the wall edges before painting.

attrs.symptom: The MDF swells and bubbles at the base of the panel near the skirting
attrs.cause: Moisture from the floor (particularly in older houses with a stone or concrete floor) migrating into the unprimed MDF edge.
attrs.fix: Prime all edges of the MDF (especially the bottom edge) with two coats of oil-based primer before fitting, and seal the base edge against the skirting with a bead of silicone.

attrs.symptom: Mitre joints in the moulding open up after a few weeks
attrs.cause: Timber movement as the room temperature and humidity changed after installation.
attrs.fix: Fill the joint with a flexible decorator's caulk to match the paint colour, then sand and repaint over the fill.
